headline: バンド is the English word “band” in katakana.

sources.quote: From English band.

headline: 楽, “comfort, ease”, is borrowed from Middle Chinese, where the source writes it 樂 (MC lak).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 樂 (MC lak).

headline: カー is the English word “car”, borrowed as it is.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English car.

headline: 遅れ, “delay, lag”, is the continuative stem of the verb 遅れる (okureru), with examples from at least the 1300s.

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 遅(おく)れる (okureru, “to be late; to be delayed; to come after something else”).
Examples appear from at least the 1300s.

headline: レクリェーション is borrowed from English “recreation”.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English recreation.

meaning: here and there, little by little
headline: 点々 is a reduplication of 点.

sources.quote: Reduplication of 点.

headline: コンクール, “contest”, is from French “concours”.

sources.quote: From French concours.

headline: “This year” is spelled with 今, “now” — but the word began with 此, “this”.

sources.quote: Compound of 此(こ) (ko, “this”) + 年(とし) (toshi, “year”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 今年 (jīnnián).

headline: A tip and a chip share one katakana spelling but two different English words.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English tip.
Borrowed from English chip.

headline: A pun or witticism is the stem of a verb for “stylish” — spelled with kanji that were fitted to the sound.

sources.quote: Derived as the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 洒(しゃ)落(れ)る (shareru, “to be witty; to be stylish or dapper”). The spelling is an example of phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), ultimately from Chinese 灑落 /洒落 (sǎluò, “confident and at ease; natural and elegant”).
First cited to the late 1600s.

headline: Kana orthography is “kana use” — and the つかい voices to づかい.

sources.quote: Compound of 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”) + 遣(つか)い (tsukai, “use”).
The tsukai changes to zukai as an instance of rendaku (連濁)

headline: Coal is “rock charcoal” — a native word that was later re-read in Chinese sounds.

sources.quote: Sinicization of 石炭(いしずみ) (ishizumi).

meaning: to permit, to allow, to approve
headline: To permit is to make something “loose”.

sources.quote: Compound of 緩(ゆる) (yuru, “loose, lax”) + す (-su, causative suffix).

meaning: to notice, to recognize, to become aware of
headline: To notice is for awareness to “stick” — つく voiced to づく.

morphemes.meaning: to stick, to attach, to turn on

sources.quote: Compound of 気 (ki, “awareness”) + 付く (tsuku, “to stick, to attach, to turn on”). The tsuku reading for 付く changes to zuku as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: “To move” may start from the sound of something wriggling.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki of 712. From Proto-Japonic *unkoku.

Likely derived as a compound of うご (ugo, a 擬態語 (gitaigo, “mimetic word”) imitative of something crawling or creeping; compare the sound shapes of roots wrig- or wig- in English wriggle, wiggle) + く (ku, verb-forming suffix). Compare also the related adverb うごうご (ugougo, “wrigglingly, squirmingly, creepingly: moving in continuous small increments”).

headline: “Skilful” is, in Chinese, “top hand” — and this reading mixes two layers of Chinese sounds.

sources.quote: /d͡ʑauzu/ → /d͡ʑɔːzu/ → /d͡ʑoːzu/
From Middle Chinese compound 上手 (dzyangᴴ syuw^X, “to have the upper hand → to gain mastery, to master something”, literally “top hand”).
This reading is likely a later innovation in Japanese after the initial borrowing. This uses the goon of jō for the first character, and the kan'yōon of zu for the second character.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Chalk has a Japanese twin in チャコ.

sources.quote: From English chalk. Doublet of チャコ (chako).

headline: Pale is “blue-white” — and the しろい voices to じろい on the way in.

sources.quote: 青 (ao, “blue”) + 白い (shiroi, “white”). The shiroi changes to jiroi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Twenty years old is an Old Japanese “twenty items” — read as a single old word, not as nijū + sai.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese はたち (patati, “twenty items”).

headline: “Time” is the moon (or month) and the sun (or day), side by side.

sources.quote: Compound of 月 (tsuki, “moon, month”) + 日 (hi, “sun, day”).

headline: “Abundance” arrived from written Chinese, and is first attested in Japanese in the 1830s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from written Chinese 豐富 /丰富 (fēngfù). First attested in Japanese in the 1830s.

meaning: again, once more, a second time
headline: “Again” is “two” plus a counter for “times”.

sources.quote: Compound of 二 (futa, “two”) + 度 (-tabi, counter for times).
The okurigana び (bi) is used to indicate the reading.

meaning: to protect; to abide (by the rules)
headline: To protect is to “watch over”, and its first syllable is an old word for “eye”.

sources.quote: Compound of 目(ま) (ma-, “eye, sight”, archaic) + 守(も)る (moru, “protect, watch over”, Etymology 2). まぼる and まぶる are alterations of まもる.

headline: A glove is a “hand bag”, with ふくろ voiced to ぶくろ.

sources.quote: Compound of 手(て) (te, “hand”) + 袋(ふくろ) (fukuro, “bag”). The fukuro reading for 袋 changes to bukuro as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: “A.M.” is “before noon”.

sources.quote: 午 (go, “noon”) + 前 (zen, “fore-; pre-”)

headline: A lens may have come through Dutch or English — Wiktionary says it can't be sure which.

sources.quote: Borrowed from Dutch lens or English lens.

meaning: to be resurrected, to be revived
headline: To be revived is, literally, to “return from the land of the dead”.

sources.quote: From the classical yodan katsuyō verb yomigaheru, itself derived from 黄(よ)泉(み) (yomi, “land of the dead, underworld”) + 帰(かえ)る (kaeru, “to return”). The kaeru changes to gaeru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

headline: An actor's lines may be a “calling out” — and the kanji came from a different, Chinese-derived word.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 競り (seri, “hawking, calling out in a loud voice”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 競る (seru), “to hawk, to call out in a loud voice”) + 言ふ (ifu, ancient spelling of modern 言う (iu), “to say”):
: */seri ipu/ → */seripu/ → /seriɸu/ → /serifu/
Alternatively, the final -fu may have come instead from 合ふ (afu), ancient form of modern 合う (au, “to do something together”) (thus, a doublet of 競り合う):
: */seri apu/ → */seripu/ → /seriɸu/ → /serifu/
The kanji spelling is from the synonymous Middle Chinese-derived daishi reading below.

headline: “Possible” is “may” plus “able” — borrowed whole from Middle Chinese.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 可能 (kha^X nong, literally “may, can + able, ability”).

headline: A memory is a “thought” that has “come out”.

sources.quote: Compound of 思(おも)い (omoi, “thought”) + 出(で) (de, “something coming out”).

headline: Lunch, or noon, is a beautified “daytime”.

sources.quote: Compound of 御(お) (o-, beautifying prefix) + 昼(ひる) (hiru, “daytime; midday, noon”).
